content: 1. Depressive Symptoms, Self-Esteem, Anxiety Symptoms, and ADHD The importance of these findings is critical, as they are derived from the original GRADE Evidence Profiles used in the Australian 24-Hour Movement Guidelines for Children (ages 5–12) and Young People (ages 12–17). Additional insights were incorporated based on updates from the World Health Organization (WHO) through systematic reviews. 2. Self-Esteem and Sedentary Behavior Self-esteem was assessed using various validated tools, including the Rosenberg Self-Esteem Scale, Culture-Free Self-Esteem Inventories for Children, Marsh’s Physical Self-Description Questionnaire, and Harter’s Self-Perception Profile for Children. General self-efficacy was measured using Rosenberg’s Self-Efficacy Scale and Schwarzer’s Generalized Self-Efficacy Scale. Social self-efficacy, both online and offline, was evaluated using the Self-Efficacy Questionnaire for Children. Academic, social, physical appearance, athletic, and behavioral self-concepts were also assessed using tools like Harter’s Self-Competence Scale and Marsh’s Physical Self-Description Questionnaire. All measures were self-reported, with some studies modifying the scales. Higher sedentary behavior was associated with lower self-esteem in several contexts: Screen time: 2 out of 2 studies found this association. Television viewing: 2 out of 4 studies reported this link. Computer use: 3 out of 5 studies showed this association, with some gender-specific findings. Video games: 1 out of 4 studies found a significant association with self-concept and self-esteem. Conversely, higher sedentary behavior was linked to higher self-esteem in specific contexts: Computer use: 1 out of 5 studies found this association, specifically for self-concept. Video games: 1 out of 4 studies found this association, specifically for online self-efficacy. Cell phone use: 2 out of 2 studies found this association, but not for global self-esteem. 3. Psychological Distress and Sedentary Behavior Psychological distress, including anxiety and depression, was assessed using tools such as the Self-Rating Anxiety Scale (SAS), the Center for Epidemiologic Studies Depression Scale (CES-D), and the Mood and Feelings Questionnaire (MFQ). Psychopathological symptoms were measured using the Multidimensional Sub-health Questionnaire for Adolescents (MSQA). Higher sedentary behavior was associated with higher levels of psychological distress: Screen time: 4 out of 4 studies reported this association. Television viewing: 0 out of 1 study found this association. Computer use for homework: 0 out of 1 study found this association. 4. Academic Achievement and Sedentary Behavior Academic achievement was assessed through various measures, including school performance, grades, standardized test scores, and specific skills like reading and mathematics. Data were collected through longitudinal and cross-sectional studies. Higher sedentary behavior was associated with lower academic achievement in several contexts: Total screen time: 2 out of 2 studies found this association. Television viewing: 3 out of 6 studies reported this link. Video games: 2 out of 6 studies showed this association. Computer use: 1 out of 2 studies found this association. However, higher sedentary behavior was associated with higher academic achievement in specific contexts: Accelerometer-derived sedentary time: 2 out of 2 studies found this association. Homework outside of school: 2 out of 2 studies reported this link. 5. Behavioral Conduct and Pro-Social Behavior Behavioral conduct and pro-social behavior were assessed using various tools, including the ADHD-IV Rating Scale, Strengths and Difficulties Questionnaire, and direct observation of time-on-task. Other measures included assessments of conduct problems, peer relationships, pro-social behavior, and antisocial personality traits. Higher sedentary behavior was associated with unfavorable measures of behavioral conduct and pro-social behavior: Screen time: 4 out of 4 studies reported this association. Television viewing: 5 out of 6 studies found this link. Video games: 6 out of 9 studies showed this association. Conversely, higher sedentary behavior was associated with favorable measures of behavioral conduct and pro-social behavior in specific contexts: Computer use: 1 out of 2 studies found this association, specifically in females. 6. Quality of Evidence The quality of evidence for these findings varied, with many studies downgraded to low or very low due to serious risks of bias, inconsistency, and indirectness. Dose-response gradients were observed in some cases, but heterogeneity in measurement methods precluded meta-analysis.
